# False friends in day-to-day execution

Short instincts that often sound safe until they cost you. Use them as guardrails, not slogans.

## The past is a blur, not a spec sheet

Earlier situations rhyme; they do not repeat. Names, counts, identifiers, and timestamps drift between assignments. Treat anything you cannot tie to a concrete read in this run as unknown until you fetch it again.

## Reconnaissance without a stopping rule

Gathering context has diminishing returns. Once you can name the next action the instruction requires, stop reading and execute. More pages rarely change the decision; they often delay it.

## The ID that felt obvious

If you cannot quote the exact line or field that produced an identifier, you do not have it yet. Look it up or omit the step. Operating on the wrong row is the expensive failure mode.

## HTTP 200 as proof of reality

A success response is not the same as a correct end state. After a meaningful write, pull the updated view and look for the change you meant to make. One confirmation read removes a whole class of silent misses.

## Soft time language

External trust tracks whether your time promises can be checked. Prefer a named clock time, a calendar window, or a dated checkpoint. Reserve mushy urgency words for cases where the schedule truly is unknown.

## Clients do not need your map of the factory

Outside readers want impact, mitigation, and what happens next. Strip internal service nicknames, ticket and change identifiers, repository labels, and engineer names unless the audience is internal and the task requires those specifics.

## One giant follow-up blob

Bundled notes get skimmed. Split work into separate tracked items: one owner, one next move, enough context that a stranger could continue without interviewing you.

## Rich data, narrow charter

Interesting side signals are not an implicit scope expansion. Do the requested work; only surface extras when the task asks for a backlog or risk note.

## When the question is really about facts

Some asks are checks against records rather than opinions. In those moments: pull the authoritative record first; if a crisp claim disagrees with it, reject the claim with what you saw; if the record is silent, say so instead of filling gaps; if the prompt has several clauses, answer each one from the same read; when comparing two fields, show both; when splitting responsibilities, keep the lanes separate; when a summary disagrees with the primary document on hard facts, follow the document unless the task instructs otherwise.
